title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — forensic/moral; habitus; ἀποστασία
pass_a_gloss: Yet I distinguish, as above, the privation of justice. For there is privation of actual justice and privation of habitual justice: that is actual violation of the law, this habitual. But again justice is to be distinguished: for it can be taken either in a forensic signification or a moral. Each again is either legal or evangelical. Forensic legal justice, because it consists in perfect conformity of the whole life with the law, is lost even by a single violation of the law. For one suffices for condemnation. Of evangelical [justice] the reason is different: since it consists in remission of sins, it is plain that violation of the law does not exclude remission of sin. But justice taken in a moral sense is opposed, as I said, to violation of the law, that is, to injustice—actual indeed to actual, but habitual to habitual. But it is asked whether actual violation necessarily induces privation of habitual justice? Distinction is needed. For the reason of the habit of natural or legal justice, such as is supposed to be in Adam, and of the habit of supernatural or evangelical justice, is different. For that neither includes hope of remission of sins, nor seems to depend from elsewhere than from man's natural faculty. And so by violation of the law it is lost. But this, because it includes faith and hope of remission of sins, and depends on another principle than the human, namely on the Holy Spirit of regeneration and the Decree of election, is not shaken off by a simple violation of the law. There is also a twofold violation of the law: one is universal ἀποστασία from God, or change of the last end; the other, any particular sin: That deletes the habit of justice; this wounds indeed, but does not destroy. Since therefore Adam's justice was legal and natural, and his sin a certain universal apostasy from God, or change of the last end, it could not happen but that as soon as he sinned he was deprived of justice, nor was there need that God by some judicial action deprive him of justice.
pass_b_english: I still distinguish, as before, privation of righteousness: actual and habitual—actual law-breaking and habitual. Righteousness itself must be split again: forensic or moral; and each either legal or evangelical. Forensic legal righteousness is perfect lifelong conformity to the law, so a single breach loses it—one is enough for condemnation. Evangelical forensic righteousness rests on remission of sins, so breaking the law does not shut out forgiveness.

Moral righteousness stands opposite injustice—actual to actual, habitual to habitual. Does an actual breach necessarily strip habitual righteousness? Distinguish. Natural or legal habit (as in Adam) neither hopes for remission nor rests on anything but natural faculty, so law-breaking loses it. Supernatural or evangelical habit includes faith and hope of remission and hangs on the regenerating Spirit and the decree of election, so a mere breach does not shake it off.

Law-breaking itself is twofold: universal ἀποστασία from God—a change of the last end—or any particular sin. The first destroys the habit of righteousness; the second wounds it but does not wreck it. Adam's righteousness was legal and natural, and his sin a universal apostasy, a turn of the last end; so the moment he sinned he lost righteousness, and God needed no separate judicial act to strip him of it.
source_text: Distinguo tamen ut supra justitiae privationem. Est enim privatio justitiae actualis & privatio justitiae habitualis: illa est violatio legis actualis, haec habitualis. Sed rursus distinguenda est justitia: accipi enim potest vel forensi significatione vel morali. Utraque rursus vel est legalis vel evangelica. Justitia forensis legalis, quia consistit in perfecta totius vitae conformitate cum lege, vel unica legis violatione amittitur. Una enim ad condemnationem sufficit. Evangelicae dispar est ratio: cum enim in remissione peccatorum consistat, palam est violationem legis non excludere remissionem peccati. Justitia vero morali sensu accepta opponitur, ut dixi, violationi legis, hoc est, injustitiae, actualis quidem actuali, habitualis vero habituali. Sed quaeritur an violatio actualis inducat necessario privationem justitiae habitualis? Distinctione opus est. Dispar enim est ratio habitus justitiae naturalis seu legalis, qualis ponitur esse in Adamo, & habitus justitiae supernaturalis seu evangelicae. Illa enim nec spem includit remissionis peccatorum, nec aliunde pendere videtur quam a facultate hominis naturali. Itaque violatione legis amittitur. Haec vero quia fidem ac spem remissionis peccatorum includit, & pendet ab alio principio quam humano, nempe a Spiritu regenerationis Sancto, & Decreto electionis, simplici legis violatione non excutitur. Est etiam violatio legis duplex: una est universalis a Deo ἀποστασία, seu mutatio finis ultimi, altera, particulare quodvis peccatum: Illa habitum justitiae delet, haec laedit quidem, at non destruit. Cum ergo justitia Adami legalis ac naturalis esset, ejusque peccatum universalis quaedam a Deo apostasia, seu finis ultimi mutatio, fieri non potuit, quin simul ac peccavit justitia privaretur, nec opus fuit, ut Deus judiciaria aliqua actione eum justitia privaret.
